passage: Miss it? Of course I miss it, Anand. I'm Tarun, and eleven-hour days, client dinners, the feeling that I was going somewhere fast, all of that was mine. My daughter is eight months old, and some evenings I sit in the nursery and grieve a life that no longer fits, then feel guilty for grieving. That guilt is the worst part. Both things are true: I love her more than I knew a person could, and I miss my old pace. For a while I pretended to feel only joy. Then I started blocking out Saturday mornings for the cycling club, no apology. I came back lighter. I still lead the design team, just differently. The old me isn't gone. It has a smaller room now, in a bigger house.

qa.a: Tarun's daughter is eight months old.

qa.q: Why does Tarun feel guilty when grieving the old life?
qa.a: Tarun loves the baby deeply, so missing the old pace feels like a betrayal of that love, though Tarun says both feelings are true.

qa.q: What did Tarun do to make time for himself?
qa.a: Tarun blocked out Saturday mornings for the cycling club, with no apology.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun had kept pretending to feel only joy?
qa.a: The grief would probably stay hidden and grow beside the guilt; Tarun says the cycling club made Tarun lighter.

grounding: A new parent misses old freedom and career pace, feels guilty about it, and finds time for personal interests so that a new identity includes the old one.
